newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar cyclone kills over 100, razes villages.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar cyclone kills over 100, razes villages.

text.p: More than 100 people were killed by a cyclone that swept through southwestern Madagascar, destroying many villages, Radio Madagascar reported on Sunday.
Officials said many thousands of people were homeless after their rural dwellings were flattened by Cyclone Gretelle which struck the area on Friday night.

Church bells sounded as rescuers recovered the bodies of victims drowned by the floods which covered wide areas after winds gusting up to 220 km (140 miles) per hour swept the southern tip of the Indian Ocean island.
"More than 100 deaths have been caused and many villages have been razed to the ground," the radio said, quoting local authorities in the disaster area.
The radio said many villagers survived by clinging to trees to avoid being blown away by the cyclone, the worst to hit Madagascar in living memory.
Others survived on the roofs of buildings surrounded by flood waters.
In the first detailed reports from the disaster zone in Vangaindrano region, the radio said serious damage was also caused in Farafangana, Vohipeno, Manakara, Midongy and other towns in the area.
Normal communications with the area had been cut and the radio quoted reports from an emergency communications centre 300 km (190 miles) south of Antananarivo.
Cyclone Gretelle wreaked havoc in a rich farming zone producing coffee, bananas, oranges and lychees before heading into the Madagascar Channel towards Mozambique.
On Sunday it was reported to be centred 450 km (280 miles) southwest of the port of Toliara, which reported only limited damage.
The interior ministry's National Relief Committee (NRC) said the first medical teams and military personnel were due to fly to the area on Monday.
"The people need medicine, emergency foodstuffs like oil and rice, and building materials," NRC secretary-general Cecelian Aurelien told Reuters in Antananarivo.
Radio Madagascar criticised the slow pace of a rescue effort and said there were no boats to reach the thousands of victims of the cyclone. Many boats had been swept out to sea by the flood waters.
With normal communications cut, there was no means of assessing the full extent of the disaster, the radio said.

On Sunday, the government set up a crisis centre in Antananarivo to coordinate the relief effort. Emergency supplies of rice were sent by road from Antsirabe, 170 km (100 miles) south of the capital. Consignments of medical equipment, tents and other items were being organised, officials said.
In France, charities appealed for funds to help the homeless in the former French colony, but French authorities said they had not received any request for aid from Antananarivo.
A government official on the French Indian Ocean of la Reunion said an air force Transall transport plane carrying a helicopter was on standby if requested for rescue operations.
He was in touch with the French embassy in Antananarivo which had not received any aid request from the Madagascar government.
Gretelle was the seventh tropical storm to hit Madagascar since the start of the cyclone season in October.
